newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu advances looking over right shoulder.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu advances looking over right shoulder.

text.p: Benjamin Netanyahu became Israel's prime minister last year with right-wingers and Jewish settlers waving placards reading "Bibi is good for the Jews".
Now about a third of his Likud party and the nationalist fringe of his ruling coalition think "Bibi is good for the Arabs".

Yitzhak Shamir, Likud's previous prime minister, began hurling the barb after it became clear Netanyahu intended to honour the ousted Labour government's commitments to withdraw in three phases from much of the rural West Bank by the middle of next year.

Right-wing cabinet ministers, members of parliament and settler leaders have taken up the cry prompting speculation that Netanyahu will have to forge an alliance with the opposition if he is to implement further withdrawals.

Netanyahu appears to have nipped a parliamentary right-wing revolt in the bud, political analysts said. His centre-right coalition is in no immediate danger of collapse. But the ideological rift and visceral personal enmities within the cabinet make any headway on the road to peace impossible without the crutch of a unity government, they say.

Netanyahu, who was nurtured on revisionist Zionism that sees all of the West Bank as part of biblical Israel, pushed the first of three withdrawals through cabinet last Friday with a slim 10-7 majority.
The cabinet approval ended any hope the nationalists had of luring their prodigal son back to the settler fold.

Netanyahu's eye is on getting re-elected. To do that he needs to capture the Israeli centre, which broadly suppports the U.S.-brokered peace agreements with Palestinian President Yasser Arafat. Netanyahu beat Labour's Shimon Peres by less than one percent in the race for prime minister and his Likud party lost one-third of its seats in parliament.
To consolidate the centre Netanyahu has seized on consensus issues such as Jerusalem and security.

The international community is in uproar over Netanyahu's plan to build a Jewish settlement between Arab East Jerusalem and Bethlehem. But in Israel only the far left, who would never dream of voting for Netanyahu, openly oppose the plan.
Netanyahu has also been able to appear tough domestically by demanding the closure of four low-level Palestinian offices in East Jerusalem, which Israel views as part of its undivided capital.

Netanyahu played similarly to the gallery over Hebron, holding out for a "better deal" than the withdrawal negotiated by Peres. In the end the agreement implemented last month was little different from Labour's but it was accepted noiselessly by the centre-right, a feat which would have eluded Peres, analysts say.
Netanyahu, with no previous experience of high office and no grass-roots Likud powerbase, is treading a fine line.
The threat of a right-wing revolt is a useful shield against pressure from the United States and Arafat but both have been exasperated by the East Jerusalem settlement plan.
Netanyahu's chances of a second term depend on his fulfilling his election promise of delivering peace with security. For that he needs Arafat, who needs more land.

"On the face of it Netanyahu is not going to be able to carry out further redeployments without cross-party support," said a Likud insider who declined to be identified. "This may mean a unity government down the road," the source said.
